So you have to develop everything through mathematical models in virtual and this is where everything [music] started in terms of virtualization in Pirelli. Hi everybody. I'm Nicolola Tangan, the CEO of the Norwegian So Wealth Fund and today I'm joined by Andrea Kasaluchcci, the CEO of Pirelli. Now if you think about it, the only thing that connects a car to the road is a tire and Pirelli has been making great tires for more than a hundred years. Today, every car in Formula 1 races on Pirellles and the tire is actually about to become more of a digital product as well. So, lots to dig into here. Andrea, warm welcome. >> Thank you so much. Thank you, Nikolai, for inviting me. >> Now, when you drive, how important is the tire? >> Well, it's of paramount importance, not only because we manufacture tires, but let's imagine tires are the only point that touch the ground in a vehicle. And so all the vehicle performance go through tires. >> So when you drive when you drive Andra, what do you how do you feel that the tire is good? So you go into your Ferrari, [laughter] right? Uh you rev it up. Uh just what what does a good tire feel like? >> Yeah. Unfortunately, I don't drive a Ferrari. Not yet. But it's a dream. I will realize sooner or later. And uh well, the first thing, the most important by far is safety. And so a good tire is able to help you in braking with a short distance in all conditions of weathers. But also the pleasure of driving and the handling and the reactivity of a car is strictly related to the performance of the tires. Clearly the more a car is a high performance car, the more the importance of tires is growing. Let's imagine electric vehicle is weighter because of the battery weight and so you need higher load index and electric vehicle has a stronger torque momentum because the electric engine has a stronger torque and so you need a better grip from a tire perspective but also electric vehicle they don't have any more the noise coming from the engine and so the the comfort is strictly related to the capability of tires to reduce the noise emissions. How do you decide what kind of grooves to put in? You know, the kind of the pattern of the tire. What is that? What is that about? >> Today we all do through virtualization. So, what do we do? uh thanks to the introduction of uh modeling and now AI in our development processes, we are able to simulate the behavior of the tire matching the target coming from the car the car producers and we adapt all the pattern design by simulations. Once we are fully convinced that the performance is matching the requirement of of the market, then we develop the physical prototype. This is helping us to reduce by 30% the time to market and to become much more effective in matching the target of the car of the car makers. >> And how do you produce a tire? >> Well, the the the production process is quite complex. Despite a tire, the old tires looks like a black uh rubber donuts. Then you will be surprised in discovering the level of technology you have inside both the development process and the manufacturing process of a type. First we starts from chemicals and so the we start to develop the compounds. Then we move all the semi-finishing and the compounds into a building process when where we prepare the secured green cover. And then we arrive into the curing process where through presses we we literally cook the tire to arrive to the target performance and then we have the finishing processes. And nowadays all these process that combine chemicals with manufacturing with a curing process is um more and more full connected and automatized. >> Where where does the raw material come from? >> Raw materials comes from everywhere. But uh when we talk about natural rubber which is based of our raw materials the vast majority of natural rubber production is concentrated in the equatorial area of the world. So if we manufacture tires in Europe, we have to buy natural rubber from these places. >> Do you make better tires than Michelam? [laughter] >> That's a very tricky question. I will not answer it, but you can make the same question to the most important car manufacturer of the world or motorsport. >> Yeah. And you do Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bentley, you do all of those. It's Lamborghini, Bentley, it's Ferraris, Maserati, McLaren, is Aston Martin, is Porsche, is Rolls-Royce. And we are in 350 uh motorsport competition all around the world every year. And is car, is Moto bike. We are sole supplier of Formula 1 since 12, 2011. And starting from next year, we will be the sole supplier of Moto GP. So why do the top prestige manufacturers choose your tire? >> But because of our technology, performance, capability to innovate, flexibility, long long-term relationship we have with them. You you look it's not a question of being better or not of others competitors is is because the business model of Pirelli and the strategy of Pirelli is very simple. We only do tires. We only do tires for consumer business. No anymore truck drives or mines or big tires. Only consumer car, motor bikes. And we lead the high value market. So we are fully focalized on these. >> Let's drill down on on Formula 1. So you supplied every Formula 1 car since 2011. Um why is that so important for you? Well, Formula 1 first of all uh it's an open air laboratory. We learn a lot. We learn a lot from a technological perspective and then we transfer everything we learn into the daily tires and daily activities. I make you an example. Uh the time to market you have to develop a tire for Formula 1 is so short. You even don't have the car available when you start to develop the new structure and the new materials for the new formula one edition for example 2027 and you have very limited opportunities to make physical test of these ties. So you have to develop everything through mathematical models in virtual and this is where everything started in terms of virtualization in Pirelli. We started to introduce these in Formula 1 and then we transferred all these capabilities and knowow into the everyday tires production and development. This is just an example. >> What's so special with the Formula 1 tires? >> Well, it's it's a tire that is fitting the most powerful car in the world. You have 22 cars running at the amazing speed. And uh the first and of paramount important tes we have is of course to assure safety and then we have to balance in between durability and performance and uh we always follows the recommendation and the the targets are coming from the Formula 1 and the FIAA and through Formula 1 we have been able to improve our brand awareness all around the world and even more the brand positioning because we communicate our products and we talk about our products every Sunday during the GP to all the the followers of Formula 1 that are growing more and more and are becoming younger uh will more balanced in terms of gender women and and men and more and more passionate. Formula 1 is doing an amazing job. >> How much faster is a fresh tire? >> It's not really a question of uh of being too fast. is more a question of being predictable and to have the right balance between durability and performance which is different uh circuit by circuit because uh they have different shape, different asphalt and so on. >> Now the mix of ingredients going into a Formula 1 tire I believe is really secret. It's a bit like the Coca-Cola recipe. No. Uh >> of course it is. No, I cannot talk about that. [laughter] Okay. If you if you had to talk about it, why what's what's really give us a hint what's some of the special things in there? >> Well, the most important ingredient we put in a tire, believe me or not, in a tire for Formula 1, but I can say in all the times we we manufacture is the passion. M >> the passion of people that manufacture and develop a product that will be a few weeks after in the most visible uh track race of the world. That's what is always rising the level of performance quality. Sorry if I'm not giving you a secret in terms of ingredient but believe me it's the most important one by far. >> I suspect the secret ingredients is love and passion. Right. So in a good Italian fashion here. Um now um what about smart tires? So you've been working on the so-called cyber tire for 20 years. What is that? >> This is a new technological paradigm is where we see the future of a high performance tires going um is a tire able to collect data and as we said before tires are the only contact point between the car and the road. And so we have unique data asphalt conditions, driving style, tire conditions and through our algorithms we are able to transform these data into informations. Which kind of informations informations that helps the braking system for example the ABS to to reduce the braking distance. Everything that is improving the driving experience first in terms of safety but also in terms of pleasures driving and comfort. >> Is this only for the supercars or is this also for normal cars eventually? you know is it's both for high performance car that is where we are already into the market with uh with cyber tire with McLaren Austin Martin Pagani and more are coming into the market but it's a bow for the future autonomous driving I make you an example Nikolai let's imagine you are driving and you have an obstacle in front of you today as a driver responsible driver. You decide if braking or steering. Tomorrow with the autonomous driving, which is already reality, this decision will be taken by a software. The key information to take the right decision, which will be data driven, 100% data driven, is the grip estimator. >> And today your decision is taken by your experience and your instinct. Tomorrow will be taken by data and software and real time. And this where the cyber tide becomes of paramount importance. >> Andrea, if we zoom out a bit and look at uh Europe, historically it was the center of the world's kind of car industry and that's changing a bit. So what is happening here? >> Wow, that's a very important question for my perspective. If you allow me, I will divide from car industry perspective and tire. From car industry perspective, what I see is that Chinese car makers in the premium segment, no doubt they have been able to grow a lot and to develop nice cars leading the market in terms of infotainment, autonomous driving, electric, electric engine. Uh cost competitive as well. But Europe has a lot of opportunity still in front of that but has to react in a way. Never forget that 100% of the prestige cars are still manufactured in Europe. The brands we mentioned before are all producing cars only in Europe. We have in Europe design, we have vehicle dynamics leading position quality and so on. So we need as industry to keep on investing on this area and to accelerate in innovation from one side. Second from my point of view we need to accelerate in improving the manufacturing competitiveness when we move from prestige into a wider premium or synergic segment. The industry has a lot of opportunity today to accelerate and is not only a question of restructuring but above all is a question of accelerating automation, digitization, electrification of the factories. Last but paramount importance has to do with the uh industrial policies. The the legislatory frame is missing. Europe declared a very ambitious target of electrification years ago in the green deal. Fine. That's fine. But then we were missing an industrial policy incentivations for new cars uh uh recharge station penetration into the market which is missing. You have a fantastic example in Norway. In Norway 90% of the new or more of the new car registration are electric vehicles. Why? You have a fantastic industrial policy exactly as China did or Holland or California, but Europe just declared the target without helping with an industrial policy. That's what we mean. >> So if you could change if you could change one thing, what would you change? >> Uh industrial policy helping and and make clear to the customers where the industry is going. Today there is a lot of confusion in Europe. the end users they don't know what which kind of of cars they have to buy and someone is talking about uh technological neutrality what does it mean theological what is the real technology alternative to electrification of the of the car park there is not in my view so it's it would be much better to fix the target and then to develop a serious and consistent industrial policies to support the penetration of electric vehicle as you in Norway. >> Tell me about the tires coming from China. >> Well, I move into the to the tire industry perspective. It's it's from my point of view, this it's tougher, even tougher. It why? Because if you manufacture a tire today in Europe, you lost competitiveness compared to five years ago. We don't have raw materials. We have to import, for example, natural rubber, the vast majority of synthetic rubber and so on. M >> you lose competitiveness if you want to export for example United States because of duties at the same time there is a huge trade down driven by Chinese brands coming into Europe so it's it's becoming tougher and tougher for a car manufacturer that's the reason why one of the most important reason why Pirelli decided to move into a high performance strategy 82% of our tonova today is concentrated ated in the high performance dies in Europe even more even more we are close to the 90%. Why? Because this segment is much more protected by the competition of the Chinese or the Asian brands. They don't have the the performance the quality the trust of the car makers we have. The competition is lower the price is higher. You can protect the value of your product. >> But don't you think the Chinese will come out with high-end tires? They are improving the performance of tires year after year. But our duty is to be always faster in innovating compared to them and compared to all the others. So the the >> the main target of Pirelli is to be always the first mover in introducing new innovation, new technology and to manufacture the best performance dies. >> But you also produce tires in in China, right? >> Yes. >> And what has that uh taught you about uh Chinese production? Well, we we are learning a lot from China. When we started the the journey was more than 20 years ago was more a manufacturing hub. So, a place to produce ties with a good cost base and being closer to the European car makers, mainly the Germans that were starting to produce cars over there. Now it becomes also a very important research and development hub because with the new car makers coming into the premium segment in China and we have a lot of of newcomers producing premium cars, we partner with them and we learn that they have different requirements. They have different approach to the performance. They look more and more for low rolling resistance even at low temperature. They look more for comfort and they want very fast time to market. And so we had to readapt our our capabilities of developing tires and manufacturing tires to the new requirements. And what we are learning now is something that we can transfer to all the other countries and >> it's a way for example to become faster in developing new tires. >> Tell me about this um the speed. I mean, we had a Xpang on the on the podcast. They say from drawing board to a finished car, it's now, you know, down to two years >> versus historically between three and five. Just what are you um what are you learning about the Chinese speed? >> Without making names, but we we we did a a tender a competition between different suppliers just to have a new a new materials. We gave to some of them the the product specification and then we we waited for the an answer. Some European suppliers came back after two months with the NDA to be signed the non-disclosure disclosure agreement just two two months to prepare the administrative parts. The Chinese came back with a physical prototype. So you can imagine I'm not saying that this prototype was perfectly matching the performance. We had to do work a lot but you you can imagine the difference of the approach. >> Speed is very important is an a key competitive advantage but is not enough. >> What explains the speed? How do you get that kind of speed? What does it take in terms of process uh systems mentality? >> It's cultural. It's mentality. On top of that they don't have legacies with supplier base with complex organization. They are very lean. They think lean and they are much more result and so they have these um uh appetite for for growing for having good results for gaining market share. So is is a cultural approach a mix of appetite of uh lack of legacies lean organization the decisional process is very fast with with European suppliers we have to >> convince a lot of people having a lot of different functions around the table while quite often in China you you find decisional process very fast one person entitled to take decision and also the responsibility of Tell me about your strategy in in the US and the Americas. You you have just announced a big investment there uh a billion dollars. What are your what are your plans? >> Well, United States first of all it remains the biggest high value market in the world. It represents roughly 40% of the high value market. And uh in United States we are growing very fast but our market share is still below the average of the market share we have for example in Asia or in Europe and so we see a lot of opportunities to grow >> but nowadays I would say only 5% of what we sell in United States is manufactured in United States 55% more or less is coming from our plant in Mexico and the remaining 40% is imported by Europe. Europe and South America. And so we want to make our supply chain more resilient, improving the local capacity. >> We decide to do it starting from our plant in Georgia in Rome that is nowadays producing a bit less than 500,000 pieces and will be scaled up up to 6 million tiles in seven years from now. >> And that's also going to help your tariffs. >> Yeah. Let's let's see we the decision was taken before tariffs and uh and every time you take a decision to build up a new plant you have to think for the following 20 30 years minimum. So of course this is helping to make the supply chain more resilient versus tariffs versus uh exchange rate volatility versus logistic cost everything that is overexposing the volatility of the supply chain that's part of the strategy but is not the major decision uh driver we had the most important is to make the supply chain more resilient at 360 degree I think that the last five years uh we all learned that uh being able to deal with volatility and unpredictability it's it's a key a key success for element >> kind of brings us to uh your leadership and the culture in the company now you worked in Pirelli for more than 20 years before you took over as a CEO so you knew the company inside out what were the first decisions you made when you became the CEO >> wow uh first yes I I I have been very lucky lucky because I my first job was in Pirell in 2002 and as as apprentice and and I have been honored of becoming CEO after in 2023 after 21 years and uh the first thing I do maybe it has been of course it has been to to to go back into the office and uh to talk to my my team my colleagues and to celebrate with them because I think that my career has been uh always supported and uh by my by my colleagues and by the team because I I'm lucky enough to to know I'm not I cannot say I know all the 30,000 people we are in Pirelli but the vast majority of them and this is giving me a lot of energy and I try to uh to give back part of this energy and the pleasure and the honor of being the leader uh being appointed by Mr. Troneti Proa the previous CEO and uh the master and commander of the strategy of the company and the board of director as a co in 2023. >> What are your most important leadership principles? My leadership I think is based on trust trust with people and the people I work with and uh I think uh the capability to listen to to different ideas to everyone because I fully realized I'm not able to take all the decisions. I make mistakes. I want to be surrounded by people uh that share the same values I have and with whom there is a full trust and the capability to listen to them and to arrive at a final decision. I think that a collaborative leadership is a key successor factor to to be able to better understand the volatility around us and to take the proper decision. Then we make mistakes. >> What are the biggest mistakes you what is the biggest mistake you made? Wow. Uh I did a lot I did a lot of mistakes. Uh from a work standpoint, I think there is not a big big mistake, but there are a lot of mid low mistakes. What I try to do is always to learn from mistakes, to allow people to make mistakes. Maybe not two times the same mistakes. That's it's risky, but to make mistakes and to learn from mistakes. Maybe the biggest uh I did is more related to my personal life. It's and it's maybe recommendation I can give to all of us and the colleagues is uh to be always able to balance the priorities and never uh ask to your friends or your family to sacrifice too much. to to be present and uh now more than before I try to be uh pre I'm not saying a good father because it's is not up to me to evaluate if I'm not or I'm a good father or not but at least to be present and to to to dedicate time to my to my childrens to stay with them that's what I maybe a mistake I did in the past I I I will not repeat in the future never >> you work too much when you were young >> I work uh a lot. Yes, I'm not saying too much but I work a lot and and uh I'm not happy to work a lot but that's the way baby if you are very very smart and very intelligent you can work less with the same result. [clears throat] In my case I work a lot for having good result but luckily results are coming. >> When do you wake up in the morning? >> Seven. I did gym 50 minutes, one hour minimum every day and I listen music during uh this time. Then I stay with my children's uh a while and then uh I go work. >> What kind what kind of music do you listen to? >> Oo uh each kind of music but above all jets. I really love uh the classical jets like Chat Baker, M Davis, uh these Ser Jets, Kings, Monsters, and classic music I love a lot. >> Uh how do you relax? >> Uh but playing with my dog, with my staying with my children and uh dreaming to come back to sailing. Sailing is my big passion, my hobby. I did a lot of sailing in the past. A lot I had also the opportunity to cross the Atlantic Ocean with a small sailing boat and is something I will do once I will have time to do it again. Seriously. >> Where is your favorite place to sail in Europe? >> The Mediterranean Sea is fantastic for sailing because it's it's don't believe is easier than the Atlantic or the Pacific because the wind is changing direction very quickly. So I think Greek islands and Sicily are two of the most uh wonderful place. >> What is your advice to young people? >> Wow, that's a very important uh point and uh I think the most the most important is uh to be passionate. You always have difficulties but once you have passion and you are really passionate for what you do you can solve if not everything vast majority of the complexity you have to deal with. And so the first recommendation is look for your uh what is really making you happy or you you think could make you happy in the future and then uh to learn from mistakes and to keep on improving in your in your journey during life. >> Andrea, [clears throat] that's a great great place to end for sure. A lot of passion uh coming out of you and your company and uh please uh keep up the good work. >> Thank you [music] so much, Nikolai. Great pleasure staying with you. >> Thank you. Really hoped you liked the episode. If you did, please like it, subscribe, and put on the notification. This really helps us to get new great guests.
